exercises.heading: 16.4. Exercises
exercises.instruction: 1, 2, 3, and 4 Evaluate the line integral by two methods: (a) directly and (b) using Green’s Theorem.

problem.paragraph: $$\oint_{C}{y^{2}dx + x^{2}ydy}$$ , $$C$$ is the rectangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {5,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {5,4} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,4} \right)$$
$$\oint_{C}{ydx - xdy}$$ , $$C$$ is the circle with center the origin and radius $$4$$
$$\oint_{C}{xydx + x^{2}y^{3}dy}$$ , $$C$$ is the triangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$(1,0)$$ , and $$(1,2)$$

$${\oint_{C}}x^{2}y^{2}dx + xydy$$ , $$C$$ consists of the arc of the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and the line segments from $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ and from $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$

exercises.instruction: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 Use Green’s Theorem to evaluate the line integral along the given positively oriented curve.

problem.paragraph: $${\int_{C}{ye^{ x}dx + 2e^{ x}dy}}, C$$ is the rectangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {3,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {3,4} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,4} \right)$$
$$\int_{C}\ln(xy)dx + (y/x)dy, C$$ is the rectangle with vertices $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,4} \right)$$ , $$\left( {2,4} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$
$${\int_{C}x^{2}y^{2}dx + y\tan^{- 1}ydy}, C$$ is the triangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$
$${\int_{C}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}dx + {({x^{2} - y^{2}})}dy}}, C$$ is the triangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$
$${\int_{C}{{({y + e^{\sqrt{x}}})}^{}dx + {({2x + \cos y^{2}})}^{}dy}}, C$$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by the parabolas $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$x = y^{2}$$
$${\int_{C}{y^{4}dx + 2xy^{3}dy}}, C$$ is the ellipse $$x^{2} + 2y^{2} = 2$$
$${\int_{C}{{({1 - y^{3}})}dx + {({x^{3} + e^{y^{2}}})}dy}}, C$$ is the boundary of the region between the circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$

exercises.instruction: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18 Use Green’s Theorem to evaluate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ . (Check the orientation of the curve before applying the theorem.)

image.alt: Details A quarter annular ring is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y plane. The annular ring is centered on the origin. An arrowhead placed on this part of the curve points clockwise. From (1, 0), a horizontal line segment runs rightward until (2, 0). An arrowhead placed on this part of the curve points rightward. The outer quarter circle, labeled x^ + y^2 = 4, begins from (2, 0) and ends at (0, 2). An arrowhead placed on this part of the curve points counterclockwise. Details A closed curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, labeled C, resembles a portion of the upper half of a parabola opening rightward. The curve begins from a point at the origin, traces a parabolic path defined by x = y^2 until a point labeled (4, 2), descends vertically downward until it meets the x axis at (4, 0), runs horizontally leftward until the origin. problem.paragraph: $${\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = {\langle{y\cos x - xy\sin x,xy + x\cos x}\rangle}}, C$$ is the triangle from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,4} \right)$$ to $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ to $$(0,0)$$

$$\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle e^{- x} + y^{2},e^{- y} + x^{2}\rangle, C$$ consists of the arc of the curve $$y = cosx$$ from $$\left( {- \pi/2,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ and the line segment from $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {- \pi/2,0} \right)$$
$${\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = {\langle{y - \cos y,x\sin y}\rangle}}, C$$ is the circle $$\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 4} \right)^{2} = 4$$ oriented clockwise

$${\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = {\langle{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1},\tan^{- 1}x}\rangle}}, C$$ is the triangle from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$

exercises.instruction: 19–20 Verify Green’s Theorem by using a computer algebra system to evaluate both the line integral and the double integral.

problem.paragraph: $${P\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{3}y^{4}},{Q\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{5}y^{4},C}$$ consists of the line segment from $$\left( {- \pi/2,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ followed by the arc of the curve $$y = \cos x$$ from $$\left( {\pi/2,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {- \pi/2,0} \right)$$
$${P\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x - x^{3}y^{5}},{Q\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{3}y^{8}}$$ , $$C$$ is the ellipse $$4x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$

Use Green’s Theorem to find the work done by the force $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = x\left( {x + y} \right)\mathbf{i} + xy^{2}\mathbf{j}$$ in moving a particle from the origin along the $$x$$ -axis to $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , then along the line segment to $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ , and then back to the origin along the $$y$$ -axis.

A particle starts at the origin, moves along the $$x$$ -axis to $$\left( {5,0} \right)$$ , then along the quarter-circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 25$$ , $$x \geqslant 0$$ , $$y \geqslant 0$$ to the point $$\left( {0,5} \right)$$ , and then down the $$y$$ -axis back to the origin. Use Green’s Theorem to find the work done on this particle by the force field $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = {\langle{\sin x,\sin y + xy^{2} + \frac{1}{3}x^{3}}\rangle}$$ .
Use one of the formulas in (5) to find the area under one arch of the cycloid $$x = t - \sin t$$ , $$y = 1 - \cos t$$ .

If a circle $$C$$ with radius $$1$$ rolls along the outside of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 16$$ , a fixed point $$P$$ on $$C$$ traces out a curve called an epicycloid, with parametric equations $${x = 5\cos t - \cos 5t},{y = 5\sin t - \sin 5t}$$ . Graph the epicycloid and use (5) to find the area it encloses.

list.item: If $$C$$ is the line segment connecting the point $$\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)$$ to the point $$\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)$$ , show that $$\int_{C}{xdy - ydx = x_{1}y_{2} - x_{2}y_{1}}$$

If the vertices of a polygon, in counterclockwise order, are $$\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right),{\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right),\ldots},\left( {x_{n},y_{n}} \right)$$ , show that the area of the polygon is $$A = \frac{1}{2}\lbrack(x_{1}y_{2} - x_{2}y_{1}) + (x_{2}y_{3} - x_{3}y_{2}) + \cdots + (x_{n - 1}y_{n} - x_{n}y_{n - 1}) + (x_{n}y_{1} - x_{1}y_{n})\rbrack$$
Find the area of the pentagon with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$D$$ be a region bounded by a simple closed path $$C$$ in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane. Use Green’s Theorem to prove that the coordinates of the centroid $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ of $$D$$ are
$${\overline{x} = \frac{1}{2A}{\oint_{C}{x^{2}dy}}} {\overline{y} = - \frac{1}{2A}{\oint_{C}{y^{2}dx}}}$$
where $$A$$ is the area of $$D$$ .
Use Exercise 26 to find the centroid of a quarter-circular region of radius $$a$$ .

solution.paragraph: $$({4a \slash 3\pi,4a \slash 3\pi})$$ if the region is the portion of the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ in the first quadrant

problem.paragraph: Use Exercise 26 to find the centroid of the triangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {a,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , where $$a > 0$$ and $$b > 0$$ .

Use Exercise 29 to find the moment of inertia of a circular disk of radius $$a$$ with constant density $$\rho$$ about a diameter. (Compare with Example 15.4.4.)
Use the method of Example 5 to calculate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where
$$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{2xy\mathbf{i} + \left( {y^{2} - x^{2}} \right)\mathbf{j}}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{2}}$$
and $$C$$ is any positively oriented simple closed curve that encloses the origin.

Calculate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = {\langle{x^{2} + y,3x - y^{2}}\rangle}$$ and $$C$$ is the positively oriented boundary curve of a region $$D$$ that has area $$6$$ .
If $$\mathbf{F}$$ is the vector field of Example 5, show that $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0}$$ for every simple closed path that does not pass through or enclose the origin.
Complete the proof of the special case of Green’s Theorem by proving Equation 3.
Use Green’s Theorem to prove the change of variables formula for a double integral (Formula 15.9.9) for the case where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 1$$ :
$$\iint\limits_{R}{dxdy = \left| \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)} \right|dud\upsilon}$$

Here $$R$$ is the region in the $$xy$$ -plane that corresponds to the region $$S$$ in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane under the transformation given by $${x = g\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)},{y = h\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)}$$ .

[Hint: Note that the left side is $$A(R)$$ and apply the first part of Equation 5. Convert the line integral over $$\partial R$$ to a line integral over $$\partial S$$ and apply Green’s Theorem in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane.]
